subject: MGMT160
title: Managing in the Age of AI: The Future Manager's Toolkit

questions.stem: Describe AI as the chapter defines it.
options: Technology that can analyse information, recognise patterns, make predictions and generate content
A robot that replaces the manager by planning, organising, leading and controlling the team automatically
Human intelligence inside a computer, with the same understanding, feelings and sense of responsibility as a person
A tool that is always correct
questions.why: AI is an extremely capable tool, not human intelligence: it predicts plausible answers from patterns, which is why it can be confidently wrong. See §9.1.

questions.stem: Identify what AI is NOT, according to the chapter.
options: Human intelligence — it has no feelings, no history with your team, no responsibility and no values
A tool — it is far more than a tool because it can learn, remember and improve by itself without any human help
Able to read faster than a person — it reads at the same speed as a trained human
Able to find patterns in large data — pattern recognition is what humans still do better
questions.why: AI does not understand customers' feelings, carry responsibility or hold values. See §9.1.

questions.stem: Identify the parts of a strong prompt.
options: Role, context, task, audience and format, constraints
Greeting, politeness, urgency, importance, thanks and a signature
Title, date, author, signature and logo
Question, keywords, examples, length and language
questions.why: Brief a tool as you would brief a new assistant. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Explain why 'write a report about customer service' is a weak prompt.
options: No role, context, audience, format or constraints — garbage in, garbage out
It is too long for the tool to process properly, so the output will be cut short
It uses the word 'report', which AI tools interpret as a request for a long document
It does not say please to the tool
questions.why: A vague prompt produces generic text that fits everyone and helps no one. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Identify what the human keeps in the planning function when AI forecasts demand.
options: The goal itself, and the surprise the past never saw
Nothing — AI plans everything once it has enough data from previous years
The spreadsheet formulas, which the human must still write by hand
The weather data, which the human collects and enters into the system
questions.why: AI forecasts from history; the human owns the goal and the unseen surprise. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Explain whether AI can motivate employees.
options: No — it helps with logistics such as fair pay and schedules, but being seen by someone whose opinion matters stays human
Yes — a chatbot's praise is as good as a manager's, because employees respond to the words themselves and not to the speaker
Yes — AI can replace the leading function, because it can send personalised encouragement to every employee every day
No — AI cannot do anything at all in the leading function, so managers should keep it out of people matters
questions.why: Recognition from a chatbot is worth exactly what it costs; AI gives the manager back the hours to motivate. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Describe the main finding of the customer-service study (Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond, 2023).
options: Productivity rose about 14–15%, with the largest gains for the least-experienced agents
Productivity fell for everyone, because agents spent more time correcting the AI than serving customers
Only the most experienced agents improved, because they knew when to trust the tool and when not to
AI replaced half the agents within a year, and the remaining agents handled twice as many customers
questions.why: AI carried the know-how of the best workers to the newest ones. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Explain the 'jagged frontier' finding.
options: Inside AI's capability people did better; on tasks outside it, those who trusted the AI did worse than those without it
AI works equally well on every task, so the more people use it the better they perform
AI only helps experts, who know enough to check its answers; beginners are misled by it
AI never helps anyone in the long run, because people stop thinking for themselves
questions.why: Confident help arrives exactly where the tool is wrong. See the Dell'Acqua et al. study in §9.4.

questions.stem: Describe what happened in Mata v. Avianca (2023).
options: A lawyer filed six court cases invented by an AI chatbot; the court sanctioned the lawyers
An airline used AI to overbook flights and was fined for leaving passengers without seats
A judge was replaced by an AI system for routine cases and the decision was later overturned
An AI tool won a court case for a passenger whose flight had been cancelled without compensation
questions.why: He even asked the AI whether the cases were real; it said yes. The professional who signs is responsible. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Explain why confident AI output is dangerous.
options: Humans read confidence as competence, and AI is always fluent — so the checking instinct switches off
AI is usually wrong, so any confident answer should be treated as false until it has been proved otherwise by a human
Fluent text is always false, because true statements are usually hesitant and full of qualifications
Confident text is illegal in professional documents, which must state their level of certainty
questions.why: A hesitant colleague triggers your checking instinct; a fluent paragraph switches it off. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Identify the four ethical fault lines of AI at work.
options: Bias in hiring, privacy, accountability, surveillance
Cost, speed, data storage and energy use
Planning, organising, leading and controlling
Fear, uncertainty, comfort with old ways and loss of status
questions.why: Trained on yesterday's hires, AI can apply yesterday's prejudices at scale, politely. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Describe the chapter's calibrated answer on AI in decisions.
options: Trust it to assist, never to decide — and run the four questions on any AI use
Trust it to decide, because it has no emotions and treats every case in exactly the same way
Never use it for decisions of any kind
Use it only for hiring, where its ability to compare thousands of CVs is most valuable
questions.why: Legal? fair? who is harmed — including those the model never showed you? the public test? See §9.6.

questions.stem: Describe the Smart Manager Rule.
options: AI replaces the manual work — never the judgement
AI replaces the manager, who becomes a supervisor of the software
AI should never be used by managers, whose job is about people
AI decides, and the manager's job is to explain the decision to the team
questions.why: Good use and bad use are about what the manager keeps. See §9.7.

questions.stem: Identify the four things that stay the manager's monopoly.
options: Communication, ethics, creativity, judgement
Typing, filing, scheduling and reporting
Forecasting, summarising, drafting and sorting
Speed, memory, volume and pattern recognition
questions.why: No one is inspired by software; values must be held; AI remixes the past; judgement with real stakes is the last monopoly. See §9.7.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's answer to 'will AI replace managers?'.
options: AI absorbs the administrative layer; managers who use AI will replace managers who don't
Yes — all managers will be replaced, because software can plan, organise, lead and control
No — nothing about management will change
Only top managers will be replaced, because strategy is the function most suited to data analysis
questions.why: The human core — direction, motivation, ethics, judgement — becomes more valuable, not less. See §9.8.

questions.stem: Select the strong rewrite of 'give me ideas to improve our café'.
options: 'You are advising the manager of a 12-person café near a university. Using three months of complaints, identify the top three causes and propose one low-cost fix for each, in a table, one page, for an owner with no business degree'
'Give me good ideas for a café, please — anything that would help us improve the service, the food, the atmosphere and the way we treat our customers, and make them as detailed as you can'
'Improve our café. We have been losing customers for some time and we need to turn things around quickly, so think about everything that could be wrong and tell us what to change'
'Write everything you know about cafés, including the things that make them successful and the mistakes that make them fail, so that we can compare our café with the best ones'
questions.why: Role, context, task, audience, format, constraints. See §9.2.

questions.stem: Classify AI predicting the Iftar rush by hour and proposing a staffing plan.
options: Planning — forecasting; the human keeps the goal
Leading — motivating the team during Iftar
Controlling — monitoring the staff during the busiest hours
Organising — setting the fairness rules for the schedule
questions.why: Forecasting demand is AI inside the planning function. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Classify AI summarising 500 staff survey comments into five themes.
options: Leading — the human keeps the motivation
Planning — the human keeps the goal
Controlling — the human keeps the monitoring line
Organising — the human keeps fairness
questions.why: Summarising feedback supports leading; being seen stays human. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a scheduling algorithm that gives all the unpopular night shifts to the newest staff. Determine what the human should have kept.
options: What the algorithm is told to optimise — fairness is a setting
The list of staff names and their contact details
The clock and the opening hours of the business
Nothing — the algorithm is always right, because it has the full data
questions.why: In organising, the routine layer is automated but fairness is a human setting. See §9.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a first-year employee with a good AI tool performing like an experienced one on routine work. Determine the pattern.
options: AI raises the floor faster than the ceiling — the gains are largest for the least experienced
AI only helps experts, so the first-year employee must have had hidden experience from an earlier job
The employee must be cheating by passing off the AI's work as their own
Routine work no longer exists, so the comparison with experienced staff is meaningless
questions.why: An opportunity in your first job — and a warning about the jagged frontier. See §9.4.

questions.stem: Determine the manager's verification rule for AI output.
options: Anything that will be filed, sent, published or decided gets checked against a source the tool did not write
Ask the AI itself whether its answer is correct and accept the answer if the tool confirms that it is right
Check only if the answer looks suspicious, since most AI output is correct
Trust it if it is well formatted, because formatting errors are a sign of poor output
questions.why: The lawyer asked the AI if the cases were real; it said yes. Check against an independent source. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Analyse who is responsible when an AI invents sources in a report an employee submits. Determine the chapter's answer.
options: The professional who signs
The AI tool
The company that sold the tool
Nobody — it was a machine error
questions.why: Chapter 3's four questions apply to what you submit under your own name. See §9.5.

questions.stem: Select the reasonable use of AI in hiring.
options: Sorting 2,000 CVs against stated requirements with bias checks, then humans interviewing a wide shortlist
AI rejecting applicants no human ever saw, so that recruiters can concentrate on the strongest candidates
A model that prefers one nationality learned from old data, because it reflects who succeeded in the past
AI making the final offer alone, so that the decision is consistent and free of personal bias
questions.why: Assist, never decide; a life-shaping decision needs a human owner. See §9.6 and §9.8.

questions.stem: Classify AI counting employees' keystrokes and reading private messages.
options: Dangerous — measuring people, not work
Reasonable — measuring work, because keystrokes show how much work is done
Reasonable — it improves productivity, because employees work harder when watched
Required by the Smart Manager Rule, which says AI should replace manual monitoring
questions.why: Measure work (response times, quality, outcomes), not people. See §9.6.

questions.stem: Classify 'copy the AI draft into the report without checking'.
options: Bad use — the lawyer's epitaph
Good use — drafting
Good use — summarising
Good use — supporting decisions
questions.why: Copy without checking is bad use; drafting then applying your judgement is good use. See §9.7.

questions.stem: Classify 'ask the AI for five options before judging any'.
options: Good use — brainstorming
Bad use — trusting blindly
Bad use — letting AI decide
Bad use — hiding the use
questions.why: Chapter 4's creativity rule, on tap. See §9.7.

questions.stem: Analyse an employee who uses AI for a report and does not declare it. Determine the chapter's view.
options: Bad use — undeclared AI is dishonesty with extra steps
Good use — declaring is unnecessary, because the tool is just like a spell-checker
Good use — if the report is correct, it does not matter how it was produced
Neutral — it depends on whether the manager has asked about AI use
questions.why: Hide the use is in the bad-use column. See §9.7.

questions.stem: Determine who should decide on firing an employee after repeated performance issues.
options: Human — AI may flag the data, but the decision, the conversation and the dignity are human work
AI — it has all the performance data and no personal feelings about the employee, so its decision is fairer and faster
Both — AI decides on the data, and the human informs the employee of the result
AI, human-checked — the system decides and a manager signs the letter
questions.why: Imagine learning of your dismissal from an algorithm — now never build that company. See §9.8.

questions.stem: Determine who should decide next month's shifts for 30 people.
options: AI, human-checked — fairness rules set by the manager, exceptions handled by a person
Human only — AI cannot schedule fairly, because it does not know the staff, their families or their problems
AI only — no human is needed, because scheduling is a routine task
Nobody — let the staff choose their own shifts freely each month
questions.why: The routine layer is automated; the human sets fairness and handles exceptions. See §9.8.

questions.stem: Analyse the decision 'should we open the second branch?' with AI scenarios and forecasts available. Determine who owns it.
options: Both — AI runs scenarios; the bet, the risk appetite and the accountability are the manager's
AI — it has all the market data and can compare far more scenarios than any manager could in a year
Nobody — wait for more data until the forecast is certain enough to act on
The employees by vote, since they will have to work in the new branch
questions.why: Strategy is both, with the human owning it. See §9.8.
